name: Estra
sentence: Leads puberty changes, mostly in girls.
shortAnswer: Estrogen is a group of hormones that lead puberty in most girls. The ovaries make most of it, and it helps shape the body’s changes and, later, the monthly cycle. Boys’ bodies make a little too. In the crew, Estra is the picture of that job: what a body does, never a measurement of your child.
whenToTalk: Talk with your pediatrician if signs of puberty start before age 8 in girls or before age 9 in boys, or if there are none by age 13 in girls or 14 in boys (the NHS draws its “delayed” line at 15 for everyone). Also check in if your child seems very upset about body changes. Anything between those ages is a wide, normal range.

locked.explanation:
## What is estrogen, and what does it do in puberty?

Estrogen is a group of hormones, the chemical messages a body sends through the blood. In girls, the ovaries make most of it. Boys’ bodies make small amounts too, and part of a boy’s testosterone is converted into estrogen.

In the crew, **Estra** stands for the hormone that leads puberty in most girls. She is a picture of what a body does, not a measurement of your child. We never guess a hormone level from a mood, a pimple or a growth spurt, and nobody can read one from the outside.

What does she help with? The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says rising estrogen causes fat to settle in the hips and breasts, so a rounder shape is part of the plan, not a problem to fix. It also causes the clear or white vaginal fluid that many girls notice about 6 to 12 months before a first period. Later, with her partner Progi, she helps set up the monthly rhythm that Ciklo stands for.

## Who tells Estra when to start?

She doesn’t switch on by herself. NICHD, the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, explains that puberty’s trigger sits in a small part of the brain called the hypothalamus. It releases a signal called GnRH, which tells the pituitary gland to release two more hormones, LH and FSH. Those travel through the blood and signal the ovaries or testes to make sex hormones, including estrogens and testosterone.

In crew language, Elfi carries that message, and Gona, the ovaries and testes, makes Estra, Progi and Teo. Teo is the testosterone character, and he has his own page.

## What is normal, and when does it happen?

NICHD says puberty typically starts between ages 8 and 13 for girls and 9 and 14 for boys. That is a wide window on purpose. A girl who starts at 8 and a girl who starts at 13 can both be right where they should be.

The AAP says the earliest sign in most girls is breast “buds,” nickel-sized bumps under the nipple. In about 15% of girls, pubic hair comes first. The fastest growth in height usually happens between the start of breast budding and about six months before the first period, then it slows. Most girls get their first period within 2 to 3 years after breast buds appear, and the average age in the US is around 12.

Boys get a little Estra too. The AAP says three in four boys, if not more, have some breast growth during puberty, because some of their testosterone converts to estrogen, and it usually goes away in one to two years. Tell your son before he wonders. Many boys are relieved to hear it.

## Does estrogen make girls moody?

No. It is tempting to say “it’s her hormones,” but a hormone’s name doesn’t explain a slammed door. The National Institute of Mental Health notes that many teens don’t get enough sleep, which makes it harder to pay attention and control impulses, and that the sleep hormone melatonin works differently in teens. Friends matter more. And the prefrontal cortex, the planning-and-braking region Fronti runs, is one of the last parts of the brain to mature.

Some girls do feel tired or sore in the days before a period. That is common, and it is real. But it is a few days in a month, not a personality. Sleep, stress, friends and a brain still under construction are the better places to look first. Calling a daughter “hormonal” can also end the very conversation she needed.

## What helps at home?

Habits, not products. Protect sleep with a steady wake-up time and phones that charge outside the bedroom. Get daylight and movement she actually enjoys. Serve regular meals of real food, and keep diet talk out of it, because a changing shape is a normal part of puberty.

Keep talking. The AAP says talking about puberty should not be a one-time discussion, and that small conversations keep the door open. Think a hundred small talks, not one big one, ideally side by side in the car or while cooking. The AAP suggests starting around the breast bud stage, before the changes are all done. Boys need the real words too: what Estra does in girls’ bodies, and a little in theirs.

Estra doesn’t need boosting, balancing or fixing. If you are unsure whether your child’s timing is typical, bring the question to your pediatrician, who can look at the whole picture. Nobody’s timing is a race.

name: Progi
sentence: Estra’s partner in the monthly cycle.
shortAnswer: Progesterone is a hormone made mainly by the ovaries. Each month, after an egg is released, it rises and helps keep the lining of the uterus ready. If the cycle ends without a pregnancy, it falls and the lining leaves as a period. In the crew, Progi is Estra’s partner, a picture of that job, never a measurement.
whenToTalk: Talk with your pediatrician if the mood or body changes before periods stop her from her usual activities, leave her very sad or hopeless, or last beyond the first few days of her period. If she talks about hurting herself, act the same day: ask directly, stay close, and call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). In an emergency, call 911.

locked.explanation:
## What is progesterone, and what does it do?

Progesterone is a hormone made mainly by the ovaries, according to MedlinePlus. Its monthly job is to help get the lining of the uterus ready, in case a pregnancy begins.

In the crew, **Progi** stands for that job. She is Estra’s partner, a picture of what a body does, never a measurement of your child. We don’t read a progesterone level from a mood, a bad night or a stomachache.

Boys’ bodies don’t run a monthly cycle, but boys share classrooms, teams and houses with people whose bodies do. It helps them to know the basics, in real words.

## How do Estra and Progi take turns each month?

MedlinePlus describes it like this. In the first half of a normal cycle, estrogen makes the lining of the uterus grow thicker. In the second half, an ovary releases an egg, and progesterone begins to rise. It helps hold that lining ready.

If no pregnancy follows, progesterone falls, the lining thins, and the body sheds the extra tissue and blood as a period. The Office on Women’s Health says very low levels of estrogen and progesterone tell the body to begin menstruation.

Then it starts again. That repeating rhythm is what Ciklo stands for, and Gona, the ovaries, makes both partners.

## Why do the first periods run on a wobbly schedule?

Because the cycle is still learning. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says it is common for teens to have irregular periods in the first 2 to 3 years after their first period. One common cause is anovulation, when the ovaries don’t release an egg. Since Progi’s rise follows the egg, in the crew picture she doesn’t always arrive on schedule in the early years.

The Office on Women’s Health adds that cycles longer than 38 days are common for a few years, and that cycles usually become more regular within three years. So a late or surprise period in the first year or two is often just the cycle warming up. No one is behind.

A paper calendar helps. Marking the first day of each period, how long it lasted and how she felt turns worry into information, and it is useful to show a pediatrician. The AAP also notes that it is rare for teens to go more than 3 months between periods, even in the first 2 years, so that gap is worth a call.

## Is a rough week before a period “just hormones”?

PMS is real. Nemours KidsHealth describes it as mood and body changes before or during a period, usually at their worst in the four days before the period and usually gone two to three days after it begins. It can mean sadness or crankiness, and also bloating, headaches or sore breasts. When a daughter is tired, tender or touchy at that time of the month, take it seriously and be kind.

But we don’t blame Progi or Estra for a hard day. A girl who is short on sleep, stressed about school or fighting with a friend has reasons that don’t need a hormone to explain them, and the teen brain is still under construction. “You’re just hormonal” also tends to end the talk. “That sounds like a rough day” keeps it going.

## What helps at home?

Habits, not products. KidsHealth lists regular exercise, balanced meals, a little less salt for bloating, less caffeine, and yoga or meditation as things teens can try, and a heating pad on the belly for cramps. Add the basics for any growing body: a steady wake-up time, phones charging outside the bedroom, daylight and regular meals without diets.

Keep the talks small and frequent. A hundred small talks, side by side in the car or the kitchen, work better than one big sit-down. If home habits are not enough, the pediatrician is the one to ask about options. Nobody’s cycle is a race, and no one needs to suffer quietly.

locked.explanation:
## What is kisspeptin, and what does Pepi do in puberty?

Kisspeptin is a tiny signal made by nerve cells in the hypothalamus, a small control center deep in the brain. It sits at the very top of the chain that starts puberty. In the crew, **Pepi** stands for that first nudge, the hand on the switch.

Pepi is a picture of what a body does, not a measurement of your child. We never guess a hormone level from a mood, a pimple or a growth spurt, and nobody can read one from the outside.

Through childhood the puberty chain stays quiet. GnRH, the start signal, is naturally low in children and rises during puberty. Then the signals pick up. Kisspeptin prods the nerve cells that release GnRH, and the chain starts to move: **Rela** sends the start signal, **Elfi** carries it through the blood, and **Gona** answers by making puberty hormones.

The chain is the same in girls and boys. What differs is the far end: ovaries in most girls, testes in most boys. And the first changes are quiet and inside. Luteinizing hormone, one of Elfi’s messengers, begins to rise slowly before puberty, usually between ages 6 and 8, long before anything shows.

## What decides when the switch flips?

The honest answer is that scientists don’t fully know. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says the trigger for puberty is not fully understood. What we do know is that inherited genes largely set the timing and speed, so family history matters, and two healthy kids in the same class can start years apart.

Food plays a quiet part. NICHD lists poor nutrition among the causes of delayed puberty, and the AAP names very low body fat, for example in some athletes or with eating disorders. That is one reason we say regular meals, never diets.

In rare cases, a gene change in the kisspeptin pathway has been linked with puberty that does not start, and in a few reports with puberty that starts very young. Kisspeptin is mostly a research topic. In one small study of 15 children with delayed puberty, responses to it varied widely, and the authors said more follow-up was needed.

## What is normal, and when does puberty usually start?

NICHD says puberty typically starts between ages 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys. The NHS says anywhere from 8 to 14 is normal. In most girls the first sign is small breast buds. In most boys it is growth of the testicles. Kids of the same age can start years apart and both be normal, and nobody’s timing is a race.

## Did I do something to flip it early or late?

This is the worry we hear most. Early puberty, starting before 8 in girls or before 9 in boys, is uncommon: NICHD calls precocious puberty rare, about 1% or less of people in the US. The AAP adds that most of the time early puberty is simply a speeding up of the normal process. Late starts often run in families too.

Because genes carry so much of the weight and the exact trigger isn’t known, it is rarely possible to pin it on one thing you did or didn’t do.

## What helps at home?

We don’t claim any habit speeds up or slows down Pepi. Habits help your child feel steady while the body does its own thing. The AAP says a balanced diet and regular physical activity support normal development. Add steady sleep, daylight and food without diets.

Then talk, in a hundred small talks instead of one big one, in the car or on a walk. If you see signs before 8 or 9, or none by 13 or 14, that is a question for the pediatrician.

Instead of: “You’re such a late bloomer.” | Say: “Your body runs on its own schedule, and so does everyone’s.” | Why: Labels like early or late stick, and nobody’s timing is a race.

Instead of: “You’re developing early, we need to watch what you eat.” | Say: “Your body is doing its own thing, and my job is to feed it well. Want to help pick dinner?” | Why: Food talk tied to body shape can turn into shame, and regular meals are fuel for any growing body.

locked.explanation:
## What is GnRH, and who is Rela?

GnRH stands for gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Nerve cells in the hypothalamus, a small control center in the brain, make it and release it, and everyone makes it. Levels are naturally low in childhood and rise during puberty.

In the crew, **Rela** stands for that start signal. Rela is a picture of what a body does, not a measurement of your child. We never guess a hormone level from behavior.

## How does the start signal travel?

When **Pepi** (kisspeptin) nudges the switch, GnRH is released in pulses, short bursts instead of a steady stream. It reaches the pituitary, a pea-sized gland connected to the bottom of the hypothalamus. The pituitary answers by releasing two hormones, LH and FSH. Those are **Elfi**’s messages, and they travel through the blood to the ovaries or testes.

Once puberty is underway, the chain becomes a loop. The hormones made further down the line, estrogen, progesterone and testosterone, report back to the brain, and the brain adjusts the signal. Rela is less a light switch than a thermostat.

## Is it the same in girls and boys?

Yes. NICHD describes one path for everyone: GnRH tells the pituitary to release LH and FSH, and those tell the ovaries or testes to make sex hormones such as estrogens and testosterone. What you see first is what differs. In most girls it is small breast buds. In most boys it is growth of the testicles.

NICHD says puberty typically starts between ages 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys, and the NHS says anywhere from 8 to 14 is normal. Rela’s signal starts quietly inside, so a child with nothing visible yet may already have changes underway.

## What if the start signal comes early or late?

NICHD explains that in one kind of early puberty the brain signals the pituitary to begin puberty at an early age. It is rare, about 1% or less of people in the US, and it affects more girls than boys. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) adds that most of the time early puberty is simply a speeding up of the normal process.

Timing often runs in families. The AAP says inherited genes largely set when puberty starts and how fast it goes, so asking relatives when theirs began is a low-key way into the topic.

On the other side, NICHD says many children with delayed puberty go on to have an otherwise normal puberty, just at a later age. Causes include family history, poor nutrition and underlying medical conditions. Sorting out which it is belongs to a doctor, who starts with a physical exam and your child’s history and may add blood tests or a wrist X-ray.

A few underarm hairs or some body odor around ages 6 to 8 is usually something else: adrenarche, a separate and common process run by the adrenal glands, not by Rela’s signal.

## What helps at home?

We don’t claim any habit changes Rela’s signal. Habits help your child feel steady while the body does its own thing: a regular bedtime, daylight, regular meals without diets, and movement they enjoy.

Keep puberty talk small and side by side, in a hundred short chats, and use the real words. Boys and girls both deserve the plain version of how it works. If you are worried about timing, write down what you have seen and when, and bring it to the pediatrician.

locked.explanation:
## What are LH and FSH, and who is Elfi?

LH is luteinizing hormone. FSH is follicle-stimulating hormone. Both are made by the pituitary gland, a small gland at the base of the brain, after **Rela**’s start signal (GnRH) reaches it. They are messengers: they travel through the blood and carry the message on to the ovaries or testes.

In the crew, **Elfi** stands for the two of them as one courier. Elfi is a picture of what a body does, not a measurement of your child. We never guess a hormone level from a mood, and nobody can read one from the outside.

## What do LH and FSH do in girls and in boys?

In girls, MedlinePlus says both signal the ovaries to start making estrogen, the hormone involved in breast growth, body hair and the start of periods. FSH also helps eggs in the ovaries grow. Later, once monthly cycles have begun, a surge of LH helps release an egg around the second week of the cycle.

In boys, LH signals the testes to make testosterone, the hormone behind facial and body hair, a deeper voice and, later, sperm production. FSH helps control how many sperm the testes make. Girls’ and boys’ bodies both make both messengers. What differs is who receives them: **Gona**, the ovaries or testes.

## When do these messages start, and what is normal?

Quietly. MedlinePlus says LH is low in early childhood and begins to rise slowly before puberty, usually between ages 6 and 8, and FSH is normally low until puberty starts. So changes can be underway inside well before anything shows, which is one reason a child with nothing visible yet is not automatically behind.

NICHD says puberty typically starts between ages 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys. The NHS says anywhere from 8 to 14 is normal. What you see first depends on who receives Elfi’s messages: small breast buds in most girls, growth of the testicles in most boys. Within that wide window, nobody’s timing is a race, and two healthy kids in the same class can start years apart.

## Why do doctors sometimes test LH and FSH?

When puberty looks early or late, a doctor may look into it. NICHD says providers use a physical exam and the child’s history, and may order tests. The NHS lists blood tests for hormone levels, sometimes a wrist X-ray to estimate likely adult height, and sometimes an ultrasound or MRI. It adds that early or late puberty is usually nothing to worry about, and the tests are there to check for an underlying condition.

In delayed puberty, for example, LH and FSH can come back low, normal or high depending on the cause, so a number only means something to a doctor who reads it with your child’s age and exam. It is not something to guess at home. A mood swing, a growth spurt or a pimple tells you nothing about either one. Sleep, stress, friends and a brain still under construction explain much more.

## What helps at home?

We don’t claim any habit changes Elfi’s messages, and we never suggest supplements to “support” them. Habits help your child feel steady: a regular bedtime, daylight, regular meals without diets, and movement they enjoy. If a blood test is coming, a short honest preview helps: what happens, that it pinches for a second, and that you’ll be there.

locked.explanation:
## What are the gonads, and who is Gona?

“Gonads” is the word for the ovaries (in most girls) and the testes (in most boys). Each has two jobs: making sex hormones, and, later on, making eggs or sperm. In the crew, **Gona** stands for the gonads as a workshop. It is where the message **Elfi** carries turns into hormones, and the hormones turn into the changes you can see.

Gona’s products are three other crew members: **Estra** (estrogen), **Progi** (progesterone) and **Teo** (testosterone). Bodies mix them. Ovaries make some testosterone and convert part of it to estrogen, and in boys some testosterone turns into estrogen too. Gona is a picture of what a body does, not a measurement of your child, and we never guess hormone levels from behavior.

## What does Gona do in girls and in boys?

In girls, the ovaries start making estrogen, the hormone involved in breast growth, body hair and the start of periods. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) describes the usual order: breast buds first for most girls (about 15% see pubic hair first), then body hair, a growth spurt, and a first period, which most girls get 2 to 3 years after the buds appear. In the US that averages around 12 or 13. Periods may be irregular for the first few years while the body adapts, and later Estra and Progi keep the monthly rhythm that **Ciklo** stands for.

In boys, the testes start making testosterone and, later, sperm. According to the AAP, the first sign is growth of the testicles and scrotum, usually around age 11 and anywhere from 9 to 14. Pubic hair follows, then penis growth, a growth spurt that peaks later, and a deeper voice just after that peak. Facial hair arrives about two years after the first pubic hair. The voice may crack for a while. Because some testosterone turns into estrogen, some boys get temporary breast tenderness or swelling. It usually settles in a year or two, and a pediatrician can take a look.

## Is body odor or pubic hair at 7 or 8 puberty?

Usually not. Cleveland Clinic describes adrenarche: the adrenal glands start making more of a hormone called DHEA, typically between ages 6 and 8, which can bring body odor, a few underarm or pubic hairs, oilier skin and acne. It calls adrenarche and gonadarche, the waking of the ovaries or testes, “two different and independent processes.” Adrenal hormones don’t cause breast or penis growth, so those signs come from the gonads and point to puberty proper. Pubic or underarm hair before 8 in girls or 9 in boys is worth showing your pediatrician.

## Do puberty hormones cause moods?

Less than people think. Studies pooling many results find only a weak link between testosterone and aggression, and we don’t blame a girl’s mood on estrogen or progesterone either. Sleep, stress, hunger, friends and a brain still under construction explain much more. “Hormonal” can also close a conversation your child needed.

## What helps at home?

We don’t claim any habit changes what the gonads make. Habits help your child feel steady: sleep, daylight, regular meals without diets, and movement they enjoy. Use the real words, ovaries, testes, period, and skip the shame about odor, acne and growth. A body at this age is not a project to fix, and boys and girls both get the same warm, plain words. Keep supplies and deodorant easy to find, and talk side by side, in a hundred small talks.

locked.explanation:
## What is the menstrual cycle, in plain words?

The menstrual cycle is the body’s monthly rhythm, and it begins in puberty. Each month the body prepares the uterus for a possible pregnancy. If one doesn’t start, the uterus sheds its lining. MedlinePlus calls a period normal vaginal bleeding that is part of the monthly cycle. The cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.

In the crew, **Ciklo** stands for that rhythm. Estra and Progi keep the beat, and Gona, the ovaries, makes them both. As always, Ciklo is a picture of what a body does, not a measurement of your child. We never read a hormone level from a date on a calendar.

## When do periods start, and what is normal at first?

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says menstruation usually starts between ages 10 and 15, and MedlinePlus says most girls start between 9 and 15. The average in the US is around age 12. Most girls get their first period within 2 to 3 years after breast buds appear.

Early cycles are rarely tidy. The AAP says it is common for teens to have irregular periods in the first 2 to 3 years. The Office on Women’s Health adds that cycles longer than 38 days are common for a few years, and that they usually become more regular within three years. MedlinePlus says most cycles last about 28 days, but shorter or longer can be normal. The AAP treats anything from 21 to 45 days between periods as inside the usual range for teens. It also lists periods that are still irregular after 2 years as a reason to check in.

A period usually lasts three to seven days, according to MedlinePlus. The Office on Women’s Health puts the average blood loss at about two to three tablespoons for the whole period. Nobody’s timing is a race. A girl who starts at 10 and a girl who starts at 14 can both be doing exactly what bodies do.

## What about cramps and rough days?

The AAP says that for most teens, cramps happen because of chemicals called prostaglandins, which the uterus releases and which cause pain. Nemours KidsHealth suggests a heating pad on the belly, and the AAP notes that exercise can sometimes ease cramps too. Girls can swim and join PE during a period.

Some girls also feel sore, tired or touchy in the days before a period. That is PMS. It is real, and it lasts a few days, not a whole personality. Estrogen and progesterone don’t “make girls moody.” Sleep, stress, friends and a brain still under construction are the better places to look first.

## How do I get ready, and how do I talk about it?

Start before the first period. The AAP says the breast bud stage is a good time to talk about the body changes still to come, and that talking about puberty should not be a one-time discussion. Think a hundred small talks, not one big one, side by side in the car or the kitchen. Say what a period is, how long it lasts, that it can come at odd times at first, and that school, sport and swimming carry on as usual.

Have supplies ready. The AAP recommends making sure your daughter has what she needs for her first period, with pads, tampons and pantiliners in her locker or backpack, and showing her how to use them before it arrives. She may be away from home when it starts.

Boys need the real words too. A period is a body process, not a secret or a punchline, and a boy who understands it is a kinder brother, teammate and friend. A paper calendar with dates and symptoms helps spot patterns and keeps her data private. If any of the signs under “When to talk to your pediatrician” show up, call. That’s not overreacting. That’s calling in backup.

Instead of: “Keep it to yourself and don’t tell your brother.” | Say: “A period is a normal body thing. You choose who you tell, and nobody in this house will whisper about it.” | Why: Privacy without shame lets her stay in charge of her own story.

Instead of: “Boys don’t need to know about this.” | Say: “Everyone should know what a period is. Here’s the short version.” | Why: Boys and girls both get the real words, and a boy who understands is a kinder friend.
